scenes.heading: Inter-Service Communication: Sync, Async & Patterns
scenes.narration: Let's look at how services talk to each other, and the central choice between synchronous and asynchronous communication.

scenes.heading: Two fundamentally different ways to talk
items: Synchronous: caller blocks for a reply (REST or gRPC)
Asynchronous: emit an event onto a broker and move on
Sync couples services in time; async trades that for eventual consistency
scenes.narration: Services can talk in two fundamentally different ways. Synchronously, the caller blocks waiting for a reply, over REST or gRPC. Or asynchronously, the caller emits an event or command onto a broker like Kafka or NATS and moves on. Sync is simple and gives immediate results but couples services in time. Async decouples them in time and space, at the cost of eventual consistency and harder debugging.

scenes.heading: Why a sync call chain cascades
steps: A calls B calls C calls D, each blocking
Latency stacks: A's time is the sum of every hop
Availability multiplies down across the chain
D slows, C's goroutines block waiting on D
C's pool drains, B blocks, A falls over
scenes.narration: Here's why deep synchronous chains are dangerous. When A calls B calls C calls D, three things compound. Latency stacks, so A's response time is the sum of every hop. Availability multiplies down, so four hops at three nines are only about ninety-nine-point-six percent up. And failure cascades: if D slows, C's goroutines block waiting on it, exhausting C's connection pool, which blocks B, which blocks A. A slow leaf topples the whole tree.

scenes.heading: Bounding a hop with a deadline
scenes.narration: The fix for cascading failure starts with bounding every synchronous call. Here a gRPC call gets its own context deadline, so if the callee is slow it fails fast instead of blocking forever and draining the pool. You also propagate context across the hop: the deadline budget shrinks at each downstream call, and a trace ID travels in the metadata so a single request is traceable end-to-end. That's what makes services deployable and debuggable independently.

scenes.text: Choreography: each service reacts to events. Orchestration: one coordinator drives each step and compensates.
scenes.narration: For multi-service workflows there are two coordination patterns. In choreography, each service reacts to events and emits its own, with no central brain, so it's loosely coupled but the end-to-end flow is implicit and hard to trace. In orchestration, a single coordinator explicitly calls each step and decides what happens next, including compensation on failure, which centralizes visibility at the cost of a coordinator everything depends on.

scenes.text: Version contracts backward-compatibly and make handlers idempotent, so at-least-once retries are always safe.
scenes.narration: The craft is knowing which style to reach for, versioning contracts so services evolve independently, propagating deadlines and context across hops, and making handlers idempotent. Because brokers deliver at-least-once, the same message can arrive twice, so idempotent handlers are what make retries safe. Get these right and a set of services becomes a resilient system rather than a distributed monolith.
